title: Dixieland and ragtime crossing, and the word jazz
summary: Hug discusses how ragtime and Dixieland styles crossed after the ODJB's hit; Allen mentions older musicians such as Papa Lane.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: it does inspire you to great things. Of course, it inspired me to really something real great, which is a question that I think you will be leading up to later on, but I'm not going to approach this until you get into it.

I remember you mentioned in another interview once, Armand, that you started to play piano at a time when the Dixieland and Ragtime styles were crossing or something like that. And could you just elaborate on that a little bit?

Well, yes. I would say that they were crossing. Of course, I was not aware of what was happening because to me it was music, as I said before. New Orleans was just New Orleans to me. I knew nothing else, and I only knew the musicians in New Orleans here, the ones I was associated with, and what they played and what they stood for. And I mean, this is the only thing that I knew. Now, as far as the styles crossing, yes, I would probably say that maybe the Dixieland and Ragtime was crossing because in 1917, 1918, the original Dixieland jazz band had already made its big hit in New York.

And I'm sure that Dixieland was then becoming the craze going into the 20s, you know, into the early 20s. And surely the music was going through a lot of changes right around that time. As far as the Ragtime, the pure Ragtime, I'm sure that the pure Ragtime was beginning to fall back of what was happening because up until that time maybe all they knew was, you know, what Ragtime was. But then when they began realizing the difference between the New Orleans music and the beat and the style and the way the New Orleans musicians played, it made a big difference. That was, as you say, that was probably where it was starting to cross, you know, right there.
And I understand the word jazz was not used then, that Ragtime was the word.
Well, as Dick knows, he, once again, I say this goes back into a technical part of the history of jazz, which has always been very...
Because what I know, I've talked to the older musicians and taped their stories, and they would remember things from when Almond was, before Almond was born.
You know, we've got guys like Jack Lane who was born in 1873.
And he remembered way back there. Long. Well, I guess when you were born, he would...
He was almost ready to retire for music.
He was about ready to retire. I would say so.
